items.title: Why Your $20 AI Subscription is Actually a Steal (The “Rent vs. Buy” Debate)
items.description:
Have you ever had that “Big Brain” moment where you were like, “Why am I shelling out $20/month for these AI subs? I’ll just go buy my own H100 GPU and run it for life!”? ????
It looks like a brilliant move. Payment one time: unlimited tokens, complete anonymity. No more “Usage Limits” notifications. Welcome to “Server Busy” notifications. But before you shell out $30,000 for this chunk of Semiconductor Real Estate, let’s perform a reality-check.

1. The Sticker Shock (The Entry Fee)

An Nvidia H100, called the “gold standard” of AI, costs $30,000. If you are subscribing to an elite $20/month AI service, it would literally take you 125 years to spend $30k. Alternatively, considering an elite $200/month service, you will still need more than 12 years to break even.
When you “save” money, by the time you’re done, the H100 will be a paper weight compared to what Nvidia has in store for 2030. Trust the math: it is already shouting, ‘Don’t. Spend. Money.’

2. The Hidden “Subscription” (Electricity & Cooling)

Buying the card isn’t the end of the bill. It’s a hungry beast.

  • Power: Running a high-end GPU 24/7 is like leaving a microwave on all day.
  • Cooling: These things get hot AF. If you don’t have industrial-grade AC, your room will turn into a sauna in minutes. 😤

When you pay for a subscription, you aren’t just buying tokens; you’re paying someone else to deal with the electricity bill and the heat.

3. The Industrial Scale Problem (The “Power Grid” Vibe)

Here’s the reality: Even if you have the cash for one GPU, you’re still just one guy with an expensive heater.

Think of it like electricity. You could buy a massive industrial generator, dig for your own fuel, and hire an engineer to keep it running just to turn on your lights. Or… you could just pay the utility company $20 a month to use their massive power grid.

The big AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) are the “Power Grid.” They have thousands of these cards linked together. When you send a prompt, you’re using a tiny fraction of a massive “brain” that no single person could ever afford to keep in their house.

4. The Memory Wall

Even with a $30,000 card, you still can’t run the “God-mode” models (like the full 1-trillion parameter giants) at home. Those models require hundreds of gigabytes of VRAM. You’d need a cluster of GPUs — a “DGX” system — which costs as much as a median house in the US. ¯\(ツ)/¯

Trying to run a frontier-level model at home today is like trying to build a private space program just to see the moon. It’s a cool flex, but it’s a financial nightmare.

TL;DR: Buying your own top-tier AI hardware today is like building a private power plant just to charge your phone. It’s cool, but it’s a total burn rate disaster.

Final Sip ☕

Unless you’re running a massive data center or you just like the sound of loud server fans while you sleep, stick to the subscriptions. The “Utility” model of AI is winning for a reason — it’s cheaper, faster, and way less of a headache.

Keep your beans, buy the service.

items.title: I've built a simple tool to visualize the road to $100k
items.description:
We’ve all heard the formula for hitting a $100k goal:

  • Sell a $50k product to 2 people.
  • Sell a $1k product to 100 people.
  • Sell a $100 product to 1,000 people.

It’s a great mental model, but in practice, I’ve realized that business isn’t a straight line. In the real world of SaaS and Digital products, that math is just the starting line.

The Reality Gap

When you move from a whiteboard to an actual launch, things get messy. You have to deal with:

  • Runtime Cost: Servers, API usage, and operational overhead.
  • Marketing CAC: How much it costs to even get a look.
  • Funnel Drop-offs: People who click but never sign up.
  • Churn: The “leaky bucket” that kills growth.

Stop Guessing, Start Visualizing

When I design strategies for founders, I find myself drafting these funnel numbers manually every single time.
It’s a grind. So, I built a Funnel Estimator to do the heavy lifting.

You plug in your goal, your price point, and your conversion assumptions. The tool then builds a visual, step-by-step roadmap. It shows you a draft for how many people you need to reach and where the critical drop-offs happen.

It’s not a magic pill, but it’s the reality check every founder needs before they burn their budget on ads.

What’s Next?

This is just the first version. I’m looking to add more variables like ad spend and churn rates to make it even more technical. If you’re building something, I’d love to hear how you map your numbers.

items.title: Corporate Jargon Part 4 | Fundraising & Growth
items.description:
Welcome back to my coffee shop! ☕
Today, we’re talking about the founders’ secret language that they employ when fundraising and seeking to grow. These terms show up on every investor call, pitch deck, and “let’s scale this thing” in meetings.

1. Pre-Money Valuation — How Much Is My Shop Worth Before Money Comes In

Imagine it this way: my coffee shop is valued at $1 million before anyone invests in it. That is pre-money valuation. It’s pretty much what the investors think the shop is worth without any other cash added on top.

2. Post-Money Valuation — How Much It’s Worth After Investment

When an investor puts in $200,000 into my $1 million shop, now the shop is worth $1.2 million. That’s post-money valuation.

Pre = before the cash.

Post = after the money.

Simple math, but this difference is what equates to how much equity investors will get.

3. Term Sheet — The Deal Menu

A term sheet is similar to the deal menu. It outlines what the investor is buying, what equity they will have, and the conditions of the partnership.
It’s not the contract itself, but it’s the blueprint. In coffee shop terminology, it’s akin to sharing a menu of “today’s specials” in advance.

4. Pivot — Switching the Recipe

Let’s say my clients suddenly don’t like hot coffee and like iced matcha. If I drop the espresso and go with matcha, that’s a pivot.
A pivot is changing direction in business when the initial plan isn’t heading anywhere. It’s survival, not failure.

5. Scalability — Can the Coffee Shop Go Global?

If I produce 200 coffees per day. And if my system is good enough that I can expand it to 100 shops without exploding the cost, that’s scalability. A scalable business is able to grow big without becoming bankrupt like crazy.

6. KPI (Key Performance Indicator) — The Scoreboard

KPIs are the most important numbers to track.
For my shop, a KPI could be:

  • Daily cups sold
  • Average spend per customer
  • Customer satisfaction score

If the numbers go up, the business is healthy. If not, it's time to fix something.

7. OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) — Setting Goals Like a Pro

It’s Simple

Objectives = What I want.

Key Results = How I’ll measure if I got it.

For Example:
Objective: “Make my coffee shop the #1 in town.”
Key Results: “Sell 10,000 cups in 3 months, hit 4.8-star reviews, expand to 2 new locations.”

It’s like a roadmap where goals and numbers meet. Btw, do keep in mind how to pronounce it properly.

8. Growth Hacking — Crazy Smart Marketing Tricks

Growth hacking is seeking cheap, creative methods to scale fast.
Example: I provide customers with free WiFi if they post about my coffee on Instagram. My shop gets free advertising, and customers have the perk.

It’s scrappy, clever, and often the secret sauce behind viral growth.

Fundraising and growth jargon may sound fancy, but it’s just the language of building big dreams.
Pre-money, post-money, term sheets, pivots, KPIs, OKRs, scalability, growth hacks they all boil down to one thing: how to grow without running out of beans.

Stay tuned for the next brew in this series. ☕

items.title: Corporate Jargon Part 3 | Equity & Ownership
items.description:
Welcome back to my coffee shop!
Today lets have a strong shot of equity talk, the stuff behind startup ownership and who gets the bag when things blow up (or burn down).

1. ESOP — Sharing the Pie with Your Crew

ESOP stands for Employee Stock Ownership Plan. It’s how startups say,

“We can’t pay you like Google, but hey, have some future millions.”

Employees get company shares as part of their compensation. It motivates them to help the company grow, because if it wins, they win.
For example, if you join my coffee shop. I give you 5,000 shares as part of your ESOP. If each share is later worth $20, you’ve got $100,000 in equity. Boom.

2. Vesting — You Gotta Earn That Piece

No one gets all their shares on Day 1. That’s where vesting comes in. It’s a timer that unlocks equity over time.
The typical setup for vesting is 4 years with a 1 year cliff.
You get nothing for the first year (the cliff). After that, you get 25%, then the rest monthly over the next 3 years.
Vesting stops people from just joining, taking shares, and bouncing. It makes people stick around to own a piece.

3. Cap Table — The Startup Ownership Map

Cap Table (Capitalization Table) is a fancy name for a spreadsheet of who owns what.

It shows

  • Founders
  • Investors
  • Employees (ESOP)
  • Number of shares and % ownership

It matters because every big decision like raising money, selling the company, or going public depends on that ownership.

4. Dilution — Your Slice Gets Smaller

Dilution happens when a startup issues new shares, usually to raise money. Everyone’s % shrinks when new shares are issued.

Let’s say I own the whole company’s 100 shares.
I bring in an investor and give them 100 new shares.
Now I own 50% of the company, not 100%.
I didn’t lose money here, I just got a smaller piece of a bigger pie.
If the company grows, my smaller piece could still be worth way more.

At the end in the startup world, salary pays the bills but equity builds wealth. Learn how ownership works, or you’ll just be working for those who do. Master the game: ESOPs, vesting, dilution it’s not just jargon, it’s your future.
I’ll catch you next time for another hot shot of startup jargon! ☕

items.title: Corporate Jargon Part 2 | Startup Metrics
items.description:
Welcome back to my coffee shop guys! I’m here with a fresh cup of coffee and a fresh batch of business jargon. Today, we’re talking about some common startup metrics that we must know, its the numbers that keep investors awake at night and founders glued to spreadsheets.

1. ROI — Did That Investment Pay Off?

ROI (Return on Investment) is self-explanatory. Basically, it means whats the percentage of return I get from investing on a business

Formula:

Coffee Shop Example:

Let’s say I spend $1,000 on marketing, and it brings in $3,000 in extra sales.

A 200% ROI? That’s a win. If ROI is negative, well… you just burned cash for nothing.

2. EBITDA — What’s the Real Profit?

EBITDA is what is the Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization (yeah, a mouthful). It tells how much money a business actually makes before taxes and loans get involved.

Example:

  • Revenue: $100,000
  • Expenses (excluding loans/taxes): $60,000
  • EBITDA = $40,000

If EBITDA is high but profit is low, it means debt is eating up cash. Investors watch this closely.

3. Burn Rate — How Fast Are You Running Out of Money?

Burn rate is how fast a business spends money before it makes a profit.

Example:

If a startup spends $50,000 per month and has $500,000 in the bank, it has 10 months before it’s broke. Btw we also call that Runway to say “Our Runway is 10months”

High burn rate = danger zone.
Low burn rate = survival mode.

4. MRR & ARR — Subscription Goldmine

  • MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue): Subscription money coming in every month.
  • ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue): The yearly version of MRR.

Example:

If my coffee shop launches a $50/month coffee subscription:

  • 1,000 customers = $50,000 MRR
  • $50,000 × 12 months = $600,000 ARR

Why does this matter?
Startups with high MRR/ARR attract investors because they show predictable revenue.

5. CAC — How Much Does It Cost to Get a Customer?

CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) tells how much money is spent to get one new customer.

Formula:

Example:

If I spend $10,000 on ads and get 1,000 new customers, my CAC is $10 per customer.

If CAC is too high, your startup is bleeding money. The goal? Lower CAC and increase profit.

6. LTV — How Much Is a Customer Worth?

LTV (Lifetime Value) is the total money a customer brings over time.

Formula:

Example:

If my coffee subscription charges $50/month, and customers stay for 12 months:

Each customer is worth $600.

A business is healthy when LTV is much higher than CAC. If CAC is $50 and LTV is $600? Profitable.
If CAC is $500 and LTV is $600? That’s a bad deal.

7. Churn Rate — How Fast Are Customers Leaving?

The churn rate is the percentage of customers who leave within a time period.

Formula:

Example:

If I start with 1,000 customers and 50 cancels in a month:

High churn means customers don’t stick around — bad news for any business. The goal? Keep customers happy and reduce churn.

8. Conversion Rate — Are People Actually Buying?

Conversion rate is how many people take action (buy, sign up, subscribe).

Formula:

Example:

If 10,000 people visit my coffee website and 500 sign up, my conversion rate is:

A higher conversion rate = better marketing and product fit.

Final Sip of Coffee

Startup metrics aren’t just numbers, they predict success or failure.
If you master ROI, CAC, LTV, and burn rate, you’re not just another founder guessing numbers, you actually know what’s going on.

So next time you’re in a pitch meeting, and someone asks about your MRR or churn rate, you’ll sip your coffee and answer like a pro.
Stay tuned for more jargon in the next article

items.title: What I Wish I Knew Before Starting a Business
items.description:
Starting a business is like jumping off a cliff and figuring out how to build a parachute on the way down. Ngl it’s like an adventure It’s exciting, terrifying, and full of lessons you only learn on the way. If I could go back, here’s what I’d tell my past self before jumping.

1. Ideas Are Cheap, Execution Is Everything

I used to believe that a great idea was enough. It’s not. The real challenge is turning an idea into something that works. Most people will never execute on an idea. The ones who do win the game.

2. No One Cares (Until They Do)

At first, no one will give a damn on your business. Not investors, not customers, not even friends. You just still need to continue moving if you believe you are right.

3. Money Won’t Solve Your Problems

You might think funding would fix everything. It doesn’t. More money just means big responsibilities and bigger mistakes if you don’t know what you’re doing. Focus on getting the basics right before chasing investment. And talking about investment always remember it could be one of the best or it could be one of the worst decisions for your business.

4. The Right People Make or Break You

Hiring the wrong team member is a slow poison. Choose people who believe in the vision, not just the paycheck. And if you have the wrong co-founder? Fix it fast or it’ll sink you.

5. You Have to Sell (Even If You Hate It)

I used to think, “If the product/Service is good, it’ll sell itself.” Nope. Selling is the #1 skill every founder needs. Learn how to convince, how to pitch, and how to close deals. Or find someone who can.

6. Failure Is the Default State

Most startups fail. That’s the reality. The question isn’t “Will I fail?” but “How fast can I learn from failure and adapt?” Treat failure as feedback, not an endpoint.

7. Try to solve problems with The Rules of Three

Trust me sometime most of your problems can be fixed with the Three why

8. Focus Beats Everything

Trying to do too many things will kill your startup. Pick one problem, solve it insanely well, and expand later. Distraction is the enemy.

9. No One Has It All Figured Out

Even the most successful entrepreneurs are just making the best guesses they can. You’re not alone in feeling lost. The secret? Keep moving anyway.

If you’re just starting out, know this: It’s hard, but it’s worth it. The struggle, the lessons, the growth it all adds up. Keep pushing, stay smart, and never stop learning.

If this hits home, share it with someone who needs to hear it.

items.title: Why Corporate Jargon Matters: The First Step to Business Fluency
items.description:
Have you ever walked into a networking event, feeling pumped, only to get blindsided by words like “burn rate,” “cap table,” and “pivot”? That awkward moment when you nod along, pretending you understand, but deep down, you feel like an imposter?

The Role of Jargon in Business

Business jargon is like an exclusive club password. At first, it may sounds weird and confusing, but once you understand, it unlocks doors. These terms aren’t just buzzwords, they exist to speed up communication. Instead of a long lines of explanation, someone can just say, “Let’s optimize our ROI,” and everyone in the room instantly gets it.

Jargon isn’t just about sounding smart. It’s about efficiency. If you speak the language of business, you’re not just an outsider listening in you’re part of the conversation. That’s why I’m writing this series. I’ll try to break down the common business and startup terms from my personal experience.

So let’s start with the basics the must know fundamentals that apply whether you’re running a local bakery or building the next billion-dollar SaaS empire.

1. Business Money Basics

Before diving into startup jargons like valuation and equity, you’ll need to understand the basic terms of business.

Revenue: The Money Coming In

Revenue is the total amount of money a business earns from its products or services. Let’s say I have a coffee shop and I sell 100 cups of coffee at $5 each, then my revenue will be 100 * 5 = $500 as simple as that.

Expenses: The Money Going Out

Expenses are the costs of running a business. This will include rent, salaries, marketing, and raw materials. If my coffee shop spends a total of $300 worth on coffee beans, cups, and staff wages, those are the expenses.

Profit: What’s Left After Expenses

Profit (or net income) is what remains after subtracting expenses from revenue.

$500 (Revenue) — $300 (Expenses) = $200 (Profit)

Two Types of Profit:

  • Gross Profit: Revenue minus only the cost of making the product/service.
  • Net Profit: Revenue minus all expenses (rent, salaries, taxes).

Loss: When Expenses Are Higher Than Revenue

If my shop makes $500 but spends $600, I’m at a $100 loss. No money left for new beans — bad news.

Break-even Point: The Survival Line

The break-even point is when a business makes just enough to cover expenses, no profit, no loss.

If my monthly expenses = $300, and I make exactly $300, I am at Break Even Point.

2. Financial Reports: The Business Scoreboard

Big businesses don’t just look at one number they track progress using financial reports.

Balance Sheet: What You Own vs. What You Owe

A balance sheet shows a company’s assets (what it owns) and liabilities (what it owes).

My coffee machine? An asset — I own it.

My shop rent? A liability — I owe it every month.

Income Statement: The Business Report Card

An income statement (also called a Profit & Loss Statement) tracks revenue, expenses, and profit over time.

Cash Flow Statement: The Reality Check

Cash flow is actual money moving in and out of the business.
Let’s say someone orders 100 coffees on credit, promising to pay later.
My income statement says I made $500, but my cash flow is $0 (because I haven’t received the money yet).
This is how businesses can be “profitable” on paper but still go bankrupt.

3. Ownership & Valuation

Shares: Slices of the Coffee Shop

Imagine my coffee shop is a chocolate cake. Right now, I own the whole thing. But I want to expand, so instead of taking a loan, I sell shares (pieces of my business) to investors.

I divide my shop into 100 shares, each worth $100.

  • I keep 70 shares (70% ownership).
  • I sell 30 shares to my friend Alex for $3,000 (30 × $100).
  • Now, I have money for a new espresso machine, but Alex owns 30% of my shop.

The more shares you own, the more control you have.

Market Capitalization (Market Cap): How Much Is My Shop Worth?

Let’s say my coffee shop goes viral, and my revenue doubles. Each share’s price rises from $100 to $200.

Market Cap = Share Price × Total Number of Shares

Since I still have 100 shares, and each is now worth $200:

Market Cap = 100 × 200 = $20,000

My coffee shop’s value doubled just because people believe it’s worth more. This is how investors measure a company’s value.

Well, we learned a lot today and I ran out of beans for now, but I’ll be back tomorrow with more business jargon and a fresh cup of coffee.

items.title: Mind-Reading Tech: Privacy Nightmare or the Next Big Thing?
items.description:
Have you ever quickly thought of something random? Maybe it has been an old song. Then YouTube instantly suggests that same song. This type of thing has happened to me often enough. I really do not know if algorithms sense my mind yet. It possibly could just be a coincidence for now. But it sure makes me wonder…

Now, imagine that happening on steroids. Not just songs, your cravings, your decisions, even your secrets, all predicted before you even realize them. That’s where mind-reading tech is heading.

How Close Are We to Actual Mind-Reading?

Over the past decade, brain-computer interface (BCI) technology has evolved from speculative science to tangible innovation. Elon Musk’s Neuralink, founded in 2016, has been at the forefront of developing implantable BCIs. In January 2024, they achieved a significant milestone by implanting a device in a human subject, pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in neural interfacing. Notably, Australian company Synchron has emerged as a strong competitor, offering a less invasive approach with its stentrode device, implanted via blood vessels. In September 2024, a 64-year-old ALS patient used this implant to control Amazon’s Alexa through thought alone, showcasing the practical potential of BCIs to enhance independence for individuals with mobility impairments. These advancements highlight the rapid progress toward integrated and non-invasive mind-reading technologies, presenting both exciting possibilities and important ethical considerations as we navigate this new frontier.
(A big credit to Perplexity Ai for the help in the research)

The Perks

If BCIs really work well life may completely change. We might get the ability to control devices such as phones and cars using thoughts. Language barriers probably will disappear because of instant mind communication. BCIs may greatly help individuals having disabilities to move or communicate. Those devices might actually restore various lost senses too. All of this sounds extremely amazing to hear.
Still, there are some possible problems though.

The Risks

Your Mind = Ad Targeting Goldmine.
Right now, companies track your clicks. Imagine them tracking your thoughts. “Hey, we noticed you were thinking about pizza — here’s an ad for extra cheese!”
Hacked Brains?!
If data breaches are bad now, what happens when someone can hack your actual thoughts?
Are You Even You Anymore, If tech starts predicting what you want before you know, at what point are you making your own decisions?

So… Is This Inevitable?

Tech like this doesn’t just stop.
Once something is doable, someone will do it.
The real question is: Who controls it?

Will it have control over us, or will get controlled by them? One thing’s for sure mind reading tech is interesting. Whether it’s good or bad it depends on how we handle it.

But who knows ¯_(ツ)_/¯
Maybe one day I’ll think about this article… and it’ll just appear on the screen.

items.title: Selling Coin for 69 | RTBRuhan
items.description:
Last week my friends and I did a cool experiment!

It came to us when we were discussing a business topic. We were discussing how much a product’s value could change because of its uniqueness.
We shared our thoughts and decided to do a little experiment to confirm them.

We weren’t sure how to go about this.
We had a lot of ideas, but in the end, we landed on the oddest one.
We decided to work on a 1 taka coin because there is nothing more uninteresting and deprived of uniqueness than a 1 taka coin (90 Coin = 1$).
Now the question is, how do we make it unique?
At first, we thought it could be sold at a higher price if it was polished like a mirror. But we were lazy AF! 😂.
Then we decided to make holes inside those coins(Yeah, “Unique”😂).
After preparing the coins from a nearby store, it was about selling them. Now we weren’t somebody with financial IQ, and we didn’t know how much we shall price it; then we decided to go for 69 taka for each coin, because why not 🤣. Oh, it was four coins of 1 taka with a hole inside. So we started targeting random people from the road and tried to sell them those “unique” coins.
Lol, my friend sold the first one, but he was offered a bottle of coca-cola instead of 69 taka 😂. And he took it! 😂 cuz we’ve already asked more than 20 people at that point. I remember the guy who brought a coin from me, and he was a teacher. While I was doing my magical marketing thing on him, his students were watching me like I was some kind of magician 😂. At least I sold a coin after that. Another one is still in my moneybag. We only sold two coins this far, and we end up concluding that,
A product is sold upon multiple variables
like Quality, Usage, Demand, Marketing, and all…
It is not that easy to manipulate over a single factor like uniqueness.
Oh! This reminds me of a quote from a meme.
“Just because you are unique doesn’t mean you’re useful.”

𝗧𝗟𝗗𝗥:- We made a hole inside a coin with the value of 1 and sold it by 69.

#RTBRuhan #Story

items.title: The Facebook Outage and Whistleblower | RTBRuhan
items.description:
Facebook has been under scrutiny for a long time. But the latest controversy is one of the most serious allegations against Facebook yet.

Facebook’s content moderation policies are designed to maintain safety on the social network, but some are concerned that they may be too strict, allowing violent and disturbing content to proliferate. The recent Facebook outage happened shortly after a whistleblower revealed identity,

Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee, leaked the documents. She leaked these documents so people could see what’s happening with their sensitive data. The document contains some important information about how Facebook is making money by selling user data. She also revealed the Facebook earns the most profit when they can promote polarization of information, hatred, or polarization of opinion. In an interview with 60 minutes, she said In the 2020 election (in which Joe Biden won) they stopped promoting the polarization of false/fabricated information, hate, or opinion in their algorithms for a “temporary” period but turned it back on after the election, which often led to the US Capitol Riot. It happened earlier this year because of Facebook. In 2017, when Facebook made a big change in their algorithm, they adopted a policy of increasing their profits by spreading hatred on the internet (because as long as you spend time on Facebook, your chances of making money will increase and the main way to keep you stuck is to give you the opposite). Many political parties then complained that we now have to adopt a lot of extremist policies for you which we might not have adopted without Facebook in normal times.

As for Facebook’s companion app Instagram, 13.5% of teenage girls think Instagram makes suicidal thoughts worse. 16% of teenage girls say Instagram creates an eating disorder. As a result, they have a negative attitude towards their bodies and become depressed due to repeated visits to Instagram.

Haugen explained everything here is happening just make user interaction longer so that Facebook can get more benefit out of that. She also said these problems are solvable if congress steps in and makes sure to respect free speech.
